The supplied citation record identifies the saved file as arXiv 2504.13868v2, posted 2026-03-16; the publisher version is not on file.
paper.one_line_finding: Among 97 analyzed UK Prolific writers (100 randomized), optional access to plot ideas from 10 GPT-4o personas did not raise story similarity: similarity to the condition centroid was 90.588 (no AI), 90.095 (1-plot) and 90.233 (5-plot), F(2, 94) = 0.573, p = 0.57 (Tables 2-3, pp. 12-13), and pairwise similarity was lower, that is diversity higher, in the 1-plot arm (-1.073, 95% CI [-1.971, -0.175], p = 0.019) but not significantly in the 5-plot arm (-0.488, p = 0.291) (Table 4, p. 14).

arms.name: 0-plot (control, human only)
arms.description: Wrote the story without supplied AI plots; control participants reporting outside AI assistance were excluded. PDF pp. 10-11 and 45-46.

arms.name: 1-plot
arms.description: Could request one pre-generated plot drawn at random from the persona pool; requesting and using it were optional. PDF pp. 10-11 and 43; writing interface, PDF p. 47.

arms.name: 5-plot
arms.description: Could request up to five pre-generated plots drawn at random from the persona pool; requesting and using them were optional. PDF pp. 10-11 and 43; writing interface, PDF p. 49.

studies.task: Write an exactly eight-sentence English story about an adventure on another planet for a teenage and young adult audience (PDF p. 45, task screenshot).

ai_tool.name: GPT-4o (version 2024-05-13) on Azure OpenAI generated the plot ideas; ChatGPT o1-preview developed the personas.
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 5, Section 2.1; PDF p. 30, Prompting the personas for plot ideas; PDF p. 11 links these pre-generated ideas to the human experiment. The year is from the printed model-version date.

The interval fields contain a Bayesian highest-density interval, not a frequentist confidence interval. test.type=other and test.value denote BF01 (null versus alternative); p_value is null. Posterior SDs are not frequentist SEs and are not entered into SE fields. The fitting unit and hierarchy are insufficiently specified to confirm the uncertainty basis; se_basis=unclear records that uncertainty is printed but its analysis unit cannot be established. The posterior HDI is retained without inferring participant-level precision. Where available, control_mean is the posterior intercept from Table S2. Other fitted arm levels are unprinted and remain null; the observed Table S3 levels are in the separate story-average records. No posterior mean is reconstructed by adding a coefficient to an intercept. The more precise Equivalence Testing HDI endpoints are used rather than the rounded model-summary endpoints.

sources.locator: PDF p. 43, Story writing by participants, individual random assignment
sources.quote: Each participant was randomly assigned to one of the three conditions:

estimates.notes: Tables 5-6 print no analysis counts. The screening form identified an inconsistency between the linguistic statistics and the analyzed assigned-arm counts on PDF p. 11 and in Table 3 (PDF p. 13). Sections 3.2 and 3.3.3 explicitly describe these as condition comparisons; the paper does not report regrouping by actual plot use, so non-random assignment is not inferred from inconsistent statistics. The reported contrast is retained with n_treatment, n_control, n_total, and n_units null; no group size is reverse-engineered or imported from the similarity analyses. The printed independent-sample t statistic uses the first table column minus the second, hence control minus treatment under these arm labels; its sign is preserved. No raw difference, standard error, interval, degrees of freedom, or standardized effect is printed. One story per participant makes the per-story SD participant-level and the independent-sample test participant-based; this identifies the observation unit without resolving the analysis counts. AI access was optional and available during writing. higher_is=other: Higher values mean more words and greater story length (elaboration); the paper does not establish that a longer story is more creative.

open_items: Per-arm randomized counts are unprinted. Only total recruitment/random assignment and analyzed arm counts are reported; no allocation counts are reconstructed.
Two-arm participant totals are unprinted. n_total remains null; n_units identifies a full-model observation count only where expressly reported.
Table 2 does not identify its parenthetical quantities or SE method. Regression SEs remain null.
Table 4 prints a fitted control baseline and SE but no fitted treatment-arm levels. These remain null rather than being calculated or replaced by observed means from another analysis.

Table S3 prints observed story-average arm means and Cohen's d but no arm SDs/SEs, pairwise degrees of freedom, or standardizer definition. The printed t and d use control-minus-treatment order under the extraction labels.
The story-average omnibus ANOVA differs between the main text and Table S3. Both are quoted in a contextual source; neither supplies a two-arm test.

The Bayesian model unit and full hierarchy are unprinted. Its posterior intercept, HDIs, and Bayes factors are retained with explicit labels, while its observation count, frequentist SEs, and unprinted fitted arm levels remain null.

Tables 5-6 report the condition comparisons described in Sections 3.2 and 3.3.3, but print no analysis counts; the linguistic statistics remain inconsistent with the analyzed assigned-arm counts. All fourteen linguistic contrasts are retained as reported with n_treatment, n_control, n_total, and n_units null. The precise analysis samples and cause of the discrepancy require clarification; no actual-use regrouping or inferred group sizes are asserted.
Actual requests for and use of the optional plots are not reported; estimates concern access offered by assignment.
No preregistration, primary outcome, or single primary similarity analysis is named. The analysis variants share the same human sample and are not independent experiments.
The latest publisher version is not on file; whether it resolves these reporting issues is unverified.

Second-round codebook case: Section 6 does not establish a measure code for the NLTK action-word, descriptive-word, named-character, and emotional-word counts or the common-word percentage (PDF pp. 12 and 15-16, Sections 3.2 and 3.3.3, Tables 5-6). The ten affected estimates now have measure=null pending a vocabulary decision. Here null records an unresolved mapping, not an unreported scoring method: the paper names NLTK, part-of-speech tagging for verbs, adjectives and proper nouns, and the English stopwords corpus for common words. The specific emotional-word lexicon or classification rule is not printed. The codebook explains null for unknown scorers but gives no explicit convention for known methods outside its vocabulary; this case remains open rather than forcing automated_score or lexical_overlap.
